lesson.title: Fewer Fields, Faster Forwarding: Inside the IPv6 Header
lesson.summary: The IPv6 header trades IPv4's variable-length, option-heavy structure for a fixed 40-byte header with only eight fields, moving rarely-used functionality into optional extension headers so routers can forward the common case faster.
lesson.body:
A packet header, the structured block of metadata that precedes the actual payload, is what every network-layer protocol uses to tell routers and the receiving host how to handle the data that follows. IPv4's header is variable in length, ranging from 20 to 60 bytes depending on whether optional fields are present, and it includes a header checksum that every router along the path must recompute after decrementing the Time to Live field. IPv6 keeps the same basic idea, a fixed block of metadata in front of the payload, but redesigns it with a different philosophy: make the common case, forwarding a packet with no special options, as fast and simple as possible.

The IPv6 header is always exactly 40 bytes, with no variable length and no options embedded directly in it. It has only eight fields, compared to IPv4's thirteen. Those eight are: Version, 4 bits, always set to 6; Traffic Class, 8 bits, similar to IPv4's Type of Service, used for quality-of-service marking; Flow Label, 20 bits, a newer field letting routers identify packets belonging to the same flow for consistent handling without inspecting higher-layer headers; Payload Length, 16 bits, the size of the data after the header; Next Header, 8 bits, identifying either the next extension header or the upper-layer protocol like TCP or UDP; Hop Limit, 8 bits, the direct equivalent of IPv4's Time to Live, decremented by each router; Source Address, 128 bits; and Destination Address, 128 bits. The two address fields alone consume 32 of the header's 40 bytes, which is why the header stays fixed-length even though the addresses themselves are four times longer than in IPv4.

The most consequential design change is the removal of the header checksum entirely. IPv4 requires every router to verify and recompute a checksum over its header on every hop, which adds processing overhead at each router. IPv6's designers judged this redundant, since data-link layer protocols, like Ethernet's frame check sequence, and upper-layer protocols, TCP's own checksum and UDP's optional one, already provide error detection, so IPv6 simply drops the field and leaves that job to the layers above and below it. This single change, combined with the fixed 40-byte length, means a router forwarding an IPv6 packet with no extension headers can process the header with far less work per packet than an equivalent IPv4 packet with options present.

Anything IPv4 handled through optional header fields, like fragmentation control, routing instructions, or security parameters, IPv6 instead handles through a chain of optional extension headers, each identified by the Next Header field of the header before it, inserted between the fixed IPv6 header and the upper-layer payload only when actually needed. Fragmentation is a good example of the philosophy shift: IPv4 allows routers along the path to fragment an oversized packet, but IPv6 pushes that responsibility to the sending host, which must perform path MTU discovery and fragment before sending, using an extension header, rather than making every intermediate router do that work.

The result is a header design that is larger in raw address size but leaner and more predictable in the work it demands from the routers forwarding it, which matters enormously at internet backbone scale where a router may forward millions of packets per second.
